### 2. Bitlab.pdf

No new skill was needed; the catalogue remains **103**. The PHP example is a documented adaptation, not the writeup's credential-table dump and not an executed database test. Its output and the Git decision table are labelled illustrative.

**Corrections and interpretation.** The writeup overstates that `post-merge` runs whenever `git pull` is issued. Its successful example is a fast-forward; upstream source separates the already-current return path, and the hook manual excludes conflicted merges. Rebase is a different integration mode. The screenshots include making the local hook executable, which matters on Linux. Modern repository-ownership checks and effective configuration must be assessed before transferring the historical sudo result to another host. A GitLab Developer label alone does not establish the effective rights on every project/branch. Deployment of an HTML comment confirms content propagation, while the later PHP callback is separate execution evidence. A database running in Docker does not by itself prove that the caller lacks client binaries or establish the caller's network namespace. The screenshot's password happens to resemble base64; the observed SSH command uses the original value, so no decoding rule was imported. Replacing `jne` with `je` reverses a condition rather than universally bypassing a username check; the screenshot shows local `su` success, not proof that root SSH login is enabled.

**Reviewed without additional skills.** Existing Nmap, Gobuster, SSH/SCP, listener and binary-inspection coverage handles the repeated tool uses. The JavaScript bookmark and GitLab browser actions are application context, not a reason to execute copied code or add a generic Linux tool skill. Ghidra and x32dbg are demonstrated through GUI/Windows actions; no Linux command-line equivalent was asserted. The PHP reverse shell, privilege-escalation hook and credential replay were reviewed as source context but neither executed nor packaged as default workflows.

### 3. Bizness.pdf

**Completed 2026-10-10.** All **14 physical PDF pages** were read. Pages 2â€“4, 8â€“9 and 11â€“14 were additionally rendered and visually inspected for commands, screenshots, source excerpts and hash conversion. Source: Hack The Box, *Bizness*, prepared and authored by C4rm3l0, dated 27 February 2024, document D24.100.272. SHA-256: `e619ec04b67c53cdaccbf4bdddcfbfd4b48fbc7fab91d870cf05c1f9c03ded1f`.

| Accepted change | Source pages and useful decision |
|---|---|
| New `feroxbuster` | 3â€“4 motivate path discovery and checking a parent route despite 404 child paths. Primary documentation supports a bounded, nonrecursive first pass, separate link-extraction control, per-directory rate limits, JSON evidence and resume/TLS conditions. |
| New `derby-ij` | 7â€“9 motivate inspection of an embedded application database with ij. The portable adaptation uses a consistent working copy, read-only SQL, schema-qualified metadata and bounded column selection, with display/lock/driver recovery decisions. |
| Enriched `hashcat` | 10â€“13 support verifying legacy OFBiz salt-before-password SHA-1 and converting unpadded base64url. The converter preserves UTF-8 salt bytes as hex and requires `--hex-salt` for mode 120, rejects malformed/noncanonical input and refuses to overwrite an existing output. |

The catalogue now contains **105 independently installable skills**. The new decision examples are labelled illustrative. The Hashcat helper remains an inline conversion in the skill; no runtime dependency on another skill or maintenance file was added. The earlier Hashcat source footer is retained below.

**Corrections and interpretation.** The many 404 child paths on page 3 do not themselves prove exposed content; the later parent/login response is separate evidence. The source's use of `-k` disables certificate validation and does not justify making it a default. Modern Feroxbuster link extraction and recursion are separate controls; `--depth 0` is unlimited, and rate limits apply per directory. The documentation's older threads/connection wording was reconciled against the current CLI/parser rather than generalized into an overall rate guarantee. Derby can run embedded or as a network server; the case's absence of a listening database port is not a product-wide restriction. Page 8's `tar cvf` makes an archive without compression, and an ordinary copy of a running database is not a guaranteed consistent backup. `READONLY ON` governs the SQL connection and does not promise zero filesystem writes while booting/recovering a working copy. Page 7's configured default hash algorithm alone does not identify all stored records. The legacy source hashes salt bytes before password bytes; base64url spelling, padding and digest length matter. The published digest converts to `b8fd3f41a541a435857a8f3e751cc3a91c174362`, with literal salt `d` represented as hex `64` by the new procedure. General SHA-1 collision weakness does not by itself explain password recovery; candidate coverage and verification cost still matter. A recovered database value and successful local `su` in the historical case do not establish other accounts' current authentication behavior.

**Reviewed without additional skills.** Nmap, curl, tar, base64, tcpdump, ysoserial and existing configuration/source inspection guidance already cover the repeated portable decisions. The OFBiz exploit delivery, reverse callback, global Java alternative changes, raw netcat transfer and root credential replay were read as case context; no such commands were executed or added as default tool workflows. A product-specific exploitation skill and a general Derby administration/backup procedure were deliberately left outside this bounded intake; all related pages were nevertheless read.

**Primary sources.** Feroxbuster's [CLI reference](https://epi052.github.io/feroxbuster-docs/configuration/command-line/), [option parser](https://github.com/epi052/feroxbuster/blob/main/src/parser.rs) and [thread-limit explanation](https://epi052.github.io/feroxbuster-docs/configuration/threads-and-limits/) were checked for expansion, rate, output, TLS and resume semantics. Derby's [connection command](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.13/tools/rtoolsijcomref22318.html), [driver selection](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.16/tools/ttoolsij97656.html), [metadata listing](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomrefshow.html), [Describe](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomrefdescribe.html), [Readonly](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomref61092.html), [MaximumDisplayWidth](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.4/tools/rtoolsijcomref12281.html), [FETCH FIRST](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.16/ref/rrefsqljoffsetfetch.html), [backup overview](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.9/adminguide/cadminbckupdb.html) and [offline-copy requirements](https://db.apache.org/derby/docs/10.9/adminguide/cadminhubbkup12677.html) support the inspection procedure. The historical [OFBiz HashCrypt source](https://github.com/apache/ofbiz-framework/blob/release18.12/framework/base/src/main/java/org/apache/ofbiz/base/crypto/HashCrypt.java), [Hashcat mode 120 implementation](https://github.com/hashcat/hashcat/blob/master/src/modules/module_00120.c), [Hashcat CLI reference](https://hashcat.net/wiki/doku.php?id=hashcat) and [Python base64 API](https://docs.python.org/3/library/base64.html) support the conversion and explicit hex-salt handling. These are documentation/source reviews, not installed-version observations.

The catalogue now contains **106 skills**. Earlier source footers from the two revised entrypoints are retained below. The existing offline-NTDS reference already handles the writeup's NTDS task and was left intact. All newly invented result examples are labelled illustrative.

**Corrections and interpretation.** The synopsis skips the password-reset stage between the initial support identity and access to the forensic share; pages 6â€“7 supply that missing step. Profile-directory names are candidate usernames, and a whitespace-split SMB listing can include headers, dot entries or truncated names; existing LDAP/GetNPUsers guidance already distinguishes candidates from verified principals. The no-preauthentication requests shown on page 4 are not password guesses. Its grep filter discards error context, which should be preserved. Page 5 mentions a rockyou run, while the displayed John command has no explicit wordlist; no candidate-list coverage was inferred from the prose. The BloodHound screenshot identifies a ForceChangePassword relationship; this is a reset operation, not evidence of merely knowing the old password. Existing collector guidance already handles legacy/CE differences and limits of the alternate DNS option.

Page 8's parser output contains NT/SHA values, not a demonstrated plaintext password. Separately sorting names and NT values on page 9 loses their associations and creates unnecessary ambiguity. The observed default `lockoutThreshold: 0` does not establish every user's effective fine-grained policy or unlimited application retries. Modern OpenLDAP guidance uses an explicit URI, authenticated transport and valid presence filter rather than importing the historical `-h`/`-p`, command-line password and standalone `*` filter. A recovered value remains snapshot evidence until a separate authorised validation establishes its current use. The denied file copy and the note on page 10 suggest encryption in that case; access denial alone does not prove EFS. The backup versions shown in prose and screenshots differ, so a recovery procedure must select the actual acquired version rather than copy the date. Page 16 demonstrates that SAM account records, cached domain verifiers and LSA secrets are distinct results. A machine's present role alone also does not prove which historical database artifacts may exist in its acquired files.

**Reviewed without additional skills.** Existing Nmap, Samba smbclient, GetNPUsers, John, BloodHound.py, Evil-WinRM and offline-NTDS instructions cover the repeated useful tasks. The rpcclient reset, CrackMapExec credential trials, Samba service/account configuration, WBAdmin/DiskShadow/SeBackupPrivilege acquisition and remote WMI/PSExec execution were read as case context. No such actions were performed. A standalone rpcclient skill for controlled account changes and Windows backup/EFS administration would need a separately scoped procedure and validation; they were deliberately deferred instead of turning a destructive historical chain into a default Linux utility workflow. This is a material-scope decision, not partial page coverage.

**Primary sources.** Reviewed Pypykatz's [project scope](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz), [LSA CLI and output handling](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz/blob/main/pypykatz/lsadecryptor/cmdhelper.py), [MSV/session structure](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz/blob/main/pypykatz/lsadecryptor/packages/msv/decryptor.py) and [core parser/result serialization](https://github.com/skelsec/pypykatz/blob/main/pypykatz/pypykatz.py). Impacket's [secretsdump CLI](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/examples/secretsdump.py) and [LSA/cached-logon implementation](https://github.com/fortra/impacket/blob/master/impacket/examples/secretsdump.py) confirm LOCAL behavior, SECURITY parsing and conditional `.cached`/`.secrets` exports. Microsoft's [resultant password policy](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/powershell/module/activedirectory/get-aduserresultantpasswordpolicy), [resultant-PSO attribute](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/adschema/a-msds-resultantpso), [fine-grained policy guidance](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/identity/ad-ds/get-started/adac/fine-grained-password-policies) and [lockout-threshold semantics](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/previous-versions/windows/it-pro/windows-10/security/threat-protection/security-policy-settings/account-lockout-threshold) support the policy interpretation. Source copies and extracted text/renders remain in ignored work storage.

**Checks actually run.** Three affected skill validators passed. Repository checks passed for **106 packages, 141 Markdown files, 189 local links and 203 Bash blocks** (syntax only), and `git diff --check` passed. No LSASS dump, registry hive or directory query was executed, and no Linux or agent evaluation occurred. **Corrections and interpretation.** Page 2's prose calls the web service Apache, while its scan reports Werkzeug. Its `10.10.11.435` RPC address is malformed. Page 14 calls `/home/keira/user.txt` a root flag; it is the user path shown in the session.

A log showing an unqualified Git helper is not sufficient by itself to prove exploitable elevated PATH resolution, and a newly downloaded local binary does not establish the restricted target binary's version or behavior. For packages, makepkg consumes PKGBUILD and builds the archive; pacman installs it. Package `post_install` scriptlets and ALPM post-transaction hooks are separate mechanisms. The dummy tar archive is not referenced by the displayed empty `source=()` recipe and is not established as necessary. `--skipinteg` bypasses checks and was not imported. The final screenshot shows both set-user-ID and set-group-ID effects; these were treated as historical evidence rather than packaged as a system-modification procedure.

**Corrections and interpretation.** Pages 2â€“3 vary an HTTP Host header; the result is virtual-host comparison, not evidence that public DNS contains those names. A 400 response from one candidate is still a response distinction worth examining. Existing Wfuzz guidance already teaches baseline controls, word-count filters and individual confirmation. Pages 4â€“8 supply the review-tag/project context and show a server version; that server version alone does not establish the SDK or model-loader version. The document's motivation says the disclosures lack CVEs, while its synopsis names them; these are historical source statements, not a current vulnerability inventory or patch assessment.

Pages 9â€“17 distinguish task metadata, artifact bytes and deserialization. The historical ClearML SDK's `get()` selects behavior using the artifact type and can fall back to a local Path. The first Path result from a `custom` artifact does not itself demonstrate double serialization; the later explicit pickle-type/Path serialization example is different. A dictionary check after deserialization cannot prevent side effects that occurred while loading. The upload transformation shown in the source is SDK logic, so attributing it solely to the remote backend is misleading. The shown artifact-metadata update is an authenticated API request for the created task; by itself it does not demonstrate an unauthenticated or cross-user fileserver write. Pages 18â€“21 show a wrapper that rejects only `OVERTLY_MALICIOUS`, yet the accepted candidate is explicitly `LIKELY_UNSAFE`. This is an acceptance-policy gap, not evidence that the scanner declared it safe. Scanner exit status, report validity and all relevant records must survive the wrapper. Modern Fickling CLI source rejects findings above `LIKELY_SAFE`, and JSON output appends a result for each stacked pickle; a stale file or single-object parser could distort coverage. The ordinary CLI decompiles symbolically, whereas the similarly named library loading functions can actually deserialize. Model accuracy and an apparently successful evaluation do not prove that loading lacked side effects.

The writeup overgeneralises old `.pt` files as tar and newer `.pth` files as ZIP. Inspect actual formats: PyTorch has multiple historical representations, and extensions do not select them. Current PyTorch documentation also changes the context of the historical `torch.load` call: since 2.6 the default is weights-only when no pickle module is supplied, with documented remaining risks. No assertion is made that current tools reproduce the historical bypass. The failed web redirects for the rendered serialization page were resolved by reading the project's documentation source.

**Corrections and interpretation.** Page 1 outlines the guest-SMB, captured-authentication, service-key, SQL and Windows escalation chain. Page 2 uses Nmap default TCP discovery before a version/script follow-up; that is not all-ports coverage. Human-output filtering and a SQL Server RTM banner do not establish complete service or patch coverage. Page 3's `tee /etc/hosts` command lacks append mode and would replace the file; it was not adopted or executed. The actual NetExec flag shown is `--shares`, despite singular prose. The later smbclient prompt names the client's default identity, so the earlier guest result does not establish that the two sessions used the same principal.

Pages 4â€“5 show an uploaded Internet Shortcut whose icon points to a literal UNC address, followed by SMB NTLMv2-SSP output. That route need not rely on name poisoning. Upload success alone does not establish that a particular person opened the file or requested authentication. The captured value is a challenge-response record, not a raw NT password hash; the PDF truncates the displayed record and therefore does not supply a usable complete fixture. Responder's unrestricted defaults were replaced with explicit mode/module decisions. Analyze mode only suppresses selected name-poisoning behavior; independently enabled SMB and other servers can still collect authentication. A running main process does not prove each requested listener bound successfully.

Pages 5â€“6 show the reported recovered credential, broad BloodHound collection and a GetUserSPNs request for `MSSQLSvc/breachdc.breach.vl:1433`. Existing BloodHound/GetUserSPNs guidance already covers bounded collection and TGS evidence. The displayed absence of a credential cache does not negate a subsequently returned TGS record. The graph's KRBTGT node and narrative about automatic rotation do not establish a password-change schedule; no unsupported rotation claim was transferred.

Page 7 uses a known service password with `pypykatz crypto nt`: this computes MD4 over the exact UTF-16LE password bytes, without a trailing null. The resulting NT key also serves RC4-HMAC, but it is not an AES key or a NetNTLMv2 response. The source ticket command omits the port displayed in the preceding SPN and changes the DC address; neither discrepancy was copied as a portable convention. The domain SID is distinct from an account RID. Current ticketer defaults include RID 500, multiple privileged groups and a ten-year lifetime; the authored fixture explicitly sets those fields. Current cache-saving code can import an inherited cache, so the scoped subshell clears that variable before creating a fresh fixture. Keytab use and current options were checked against upstream code; the source screenshot is an older Impacket version.

Pages 8â€“9 show a saved cache and SQL connection. A TLS-upgrade message is not successful SQL authentication, and a saved ticket does not prove its signature or target acceptance. The SQL prompt identifies a login/database context; it does not identify the OS token used by a command launched by the service. The source changes advanced options and xp_cmdshell with RECONFIGURE, then prints the service-account identity. The accompanying NULL row does not invalidate the preceding identity row. Current helpers also change advanced options, so disabling a helper is not proof that original configuration was restored.

Page 10 shows SeImpersonatePrivilege and a Windows-only GodPotato payload followed by a SYSTEM callback. A listed privilege alone is not proof that a particular exploit is compatible with every Windows version or service context. PowerShell's `curl` spelling is not evidence of GNU curl semantics. These observations were read for context; no payload, reverse connection, privileged service change or target authentication was executed.

Its possible suffixes are bounded by distinct username characters, rather than a large random secret space. The script labels every non-302 response a valid session; that heuristic also admits errors or denials and was not adopted. PHP's Location header does not itself terminate execution. A candidate identifier only retrieves authenticated state if the application has corresponding saved session data; constructing the identifier does not populate that state.

Pages 15â€“16 show why access to the file-management page did not establish upload permission: the handler separately checks a nested JWT username and the server session. **Coverage and corrections.** Pages 1â€“2 identify the case and show all-TCP discovery followed by service/script scanning. The screenshot reports Nginx 1.18.0 with HTTP 401 and ActiveMQ OpenWire 5.15.15 on TCP 61616. These are separate services; the HTTP response does not establish OpenWire authentication. The search phrase on page 2 incorrectly says CVE-2023-46606; the surrounding explanation, linked repository and Apache advisory identify **CVE-2023-46604**. Apache describes the Java OpenWire marshaller and affected clients as well as brokers, with branch fixes including 5.15.16. The version banner remains evidence to corroborate against the deployed build, not a reason to execute a proof of concept.

Pages 3â€“4 show generation of an ELF callback, a Spring XML payload, a Python HTTP server, Netcat and execution of a Go proof of concept. The embedded download uses `curl -s` without HTTP failure handling, and semicolons do not gate later commands on download success. The sender's packet message alone does not prove target execution. The separate listener screenshot includes a PTY command and `uid=1000(activemq)`, which support the historical case's reported session. These screenshots were read directly because extraction omitted the results. Existing Go, Python server, Ncat and script guidance already covers the reusable mechanics; no payload was executed or retained as a new recipe.

Page 5's screenshot shows `(ALL : ALL) NOPASSWD: /usr/sbin/nginx` without an argument restriction. The important authority is selecting configuration and its included/native resources, not merely skipping a password prompt. The source then combines root workers, a filesystem-wide HTTP root and DAV PUT; these are distinct directives and prerequisites. Nginx `user` controls workers, while `root` maps request paths. Neither a parent master running as root nor a root-looking path alone establishes the request's actual permissions. The general skill teaches those distinctions without providing the privileged replacement configuration.

Pages 5â€“6 start an additional instance through `-c`; that is not a test or reload of an existing master. The `ss` output shows an IPv4 wildcard listener on 1337 with no process details. It does not prove ownership, which configuration is loaded, remote reachability or successful writes. The source leaves parent-directory creation unspecified; standard DAV defaults require existing parents unless `create_full_put_path` is enabled. Included-module availability, request-body temporary storage and destination permissions remain consequential conditions. Existing ss guidance already covers socket visibility and namespace limits.

Pages 6â€“7 create an SSH key pair, issue a PUT and show a later root SSH identity. The source uses shell command substitution to construct the body, which removes trailing newlines, and does not capture an HTTP status. Curl's quiet completion alone would be insufficient write evidence; the later displayed `uid=0` is separate historical evidence. PUT can replace the destination rather than append a line. The accepted upload example uses a user-selected ordinary file/URL and explains byte preservation and uncertain outcomes, without reproducing an authorized_keys write or attempting a login.

**Reviewed without changes / deliberately deferred.** Existing Nmap, Go, Python HTTP server, Ncat, script, ss, SSH and ssh-keygen cover recurring selection, scope, session and transfer decisions. ActiveMQ appears as a remote service and proof-of-concept target, not an administrative CLI workflow; no generic ActiveMQ skill was invented. The source's exploit download/build, msfvenom callback, Spring process launch, privileged Nginx startup, credential-file replacement and root login were studied as context and deliberately not executed or packaged as new payload instructions. No pages were left unread.

Upstream [nginx.c](https://github.com/nginx/nginx/blob/master/src/core/nginx.c) confirmed the configuration-test path, dynamic module loader and ignored `user` directive with a non-root master. Pages 15â€“16 show pspy v1.2.0 observing UID 0 commands, including a timeout-wrapped Bash renewal job. UID metadata does not itself prove script-file ownership, writability or exact argv boundaries. The displayed `bash -c` command line lacks preserved argument boundaries, so the caller's source is needed before inferring which value reached the script as `$1`.

Pages 16â€“18 show the renewal excerpt, a one-day generated certificate, a command-bearing subject and later root identity. The script treats any nonzero checkend result as a path toward renewal, even though malformed input also produces nonzero. Its own `exit 1` for 'no need to renew' is the wrapper's convention, not OpenSSL's success convention. The injection arises when certificate text is reparsed by a child Bash; OpenSSL does not execute the CN. The source's `-keyout /dev/null` discards the private key and does not produce a reusable certificate/key pair; current OpenSSL documents `-nodes` as a deprecated synonym for `-noenc`. The later file ownership and root callback are historical observations only, not tests run here.

Pages 5â€“6 build the purported PNG prefix as a Python 3 Unicode string containing seven characters followed by a newline. That final newline makes eight characters, but UTF-8 encoding expands U+0089 to two bytes. Current Requests passes string-valued file content into urllib3's multipart encoder, whose string writer uses UTF-8; under that path the prefix becomes nine bytes starting `c2 89`. The W3C signature is eight bytes starting `89 50`, and even its exact presence does not make a complete PNG. The historical library versions and transmitted body were not supplied, so this is a source-supported current behavior and a reproduction caveat, not a recovered packet capture. The source's unconditional `Uploaded!` print does not check the HTTP or application result. Later screenshots report command execution, which is separate evidence from the claimed image-validation explanation.

Pages 6â€“7 show curl requests, a temporary HTTP server, a downloaded Windows Netcat executable and the reported session as `buff\shaun`. They were read without sending requests, transferring executables or starting listeners. No web-shell body or case credential was added to the skills.

The installer filename is a version lead, while that netstat output alone does not identify the owning process or running build. The PDF describes a local installation in a VM but supplies no debugger derivation of the later offset/address.

Page 9 calls the connection a SOCKS proxy, but its remote syntax specifies a fixed reverse TCP forward to client loopback port 8888. It also says port 8080 in prose while the command uses 8888; the Chisel transport uses 9999. The displayed connection message establishes transport progress, not an application response. The accepted skill already used explicit loopback binding, authentication and a trusted fingerprint; those conditions were preserved.

Pages 9â€“10 display a generated reverse payload with callback port 4444, then a listener on 2222 and a reported administrator session. The callback host also differs from the earlier Chisel server host. Different hosts can be intentional, but the PDF does not reconcile this sequence, and the differing ports cannot be silently treated as one verified transcript. A fixed forward does not automatically rewrite a separate outbound connection's endpoint.

Page 11 supplies the complete appendix code: fixed padding, a hard-coded return address, payload bytes, a remaining-length calculation and a socket send. It was read as source evidence without execution. These build-specific constants and the source's Python 2 invocation do not demonstrate a portable exploit or a validated debugging workflow.

Pages 13â€“16 describe five application-side execution routes, including file editing, uploads, document templates and legacy exploit scripts. Page 17 shows an interactive shell and a local account switch. Its success does not retroactively explain the earlier SSH failure because authentication paths and policy can differ. Pages 18â€“19 then show Memcached statistics, key listing and a selected value. The displayed STAT items:1:number 5 means five stored items in slab class 1, contrary to the prose's claim of a single item numbered 1. The zero in stats cachedump 1 0 removes the requested item-count limit; server implementation limits still apply. Current upstream walks the cold LRU and caps the response buffer, so this legacy listing is not a complete inventory. The VALUE header's zero is opaque flags and its nine is a byte count excluding framing. One quit closes the connection; sending it twice is not a protocol requirement. Cached authentication-looking data does not itself prove that any login is currently valid.

Pages 19â€“21 show docker group membership, an Ubuntu image, a host-root bind mount, chroot and a reported root password change/login. The explanation incorrectly relies on the Docker client being SUID. A rootful daemon's authority and access to its API/socket explain the relevant privilege boundary. The appended PHP statement is also printed without a terminating semicolon; its complete surrounding source would be required to establish executable syntax. The reported root shell is retained as a separate case outcome, not proof that every printed fragment runs unchanged.

Existing Nmap, ffuf, grep, base64, SQLite, curl, Python, SSH, key inspection, permissions and listener guidance covers the remaining ordinary CLI uses; it was not duplicated solely to add examples.

**Page coverage and corrections.** Pages 1â€“3 give the attack narrative, a top-1000 TCP scan, exposed Git metadata, the downloader and web enumeration. The scan's two open ports describe that tested set, not all possible listeners. A denied `.git/` index does not make individual objects inaccessible. Current upstream git-dumper invokes Git checkout automatically, modifies potentially unsafe config lines and warns that attacker-controlled content can execute locally. Its normal HTTP sessions disable certificate verification, and its non-directory-listing path ignores checkout status. The accepted skill therefore separates endpoint identity, isolation, transfer status and recovered-object completeness; no downloader invocation was performed. Config sanitization also means its output cannot be described as an untouched copy of every source byte.

Pages 4â€“6 show registration, a GET request with credentials in its query string and an upload result. HTTP method alone does not establish the backend's account-lookup/create logic. A query string can be recorded by the configured log format; it is not proof that every service logs passwords. A success message and an uploaded filename are distinct from a complete image decode and successful review.

Pages 7â€“9 compare a blacklist and different HTML output paths, then build an event-handler payload. The prose sometimes calls this a filename injection, but the illustrated altered `alt` attribute and multipart `cat_name` field show the display-name flow; the image filename is separate. The accepted PHP guidance preserves that distinction and explains why encoding on the admin list does not establish encoding on the detail page. Browser entity decoding, event triggering, cookie collection and image corruption were read as source evidence and were not executed or packaged as a new CLI utility. Existing binary/upload guidance already separates GIF/PNG labels and prefixes from valid image content.

Pages 10â€“12 show the recovered browser session, a concatenated INSERT, separately bound DELETE, SQLite ATTACH statements and a web-shell/reverse-connection sequence. The later bound statement does not protect the earlier concatenation. ATTACH is a database/file operation, not intrinsic OS command execution: the historical outcome also depends on the application's SQL API, filesystem permissions, served path and PHP execution mapping. The initial generic file path and adapted application path differ. Binary-looking response prefixes should be captured to a file rather than forced to a terminal. No SQL injection, database write, web shell, server, reverse connection or payload execution was attempted.

Pages 13â€“15 export users, transform delimiters, run John, inspect groups and read Apache logs. Raw-MD5 was not selected from length alone in the new guidance; identical-length NT or other records require origin evidence. The displayed export has ten rows while the loader reports nine records; the source does not supply enough run state to resolve that difference. The skill already separates loader input, duplicate/pot state and `--show` results, now with an explicit record-association reminder. A home-directory name or database account is not automatically an OS login identity. The log directory and files show group ownership plus usable permission bits; the name `adm` alone is not a universal read grant. A logged submitted value and a redirect response are not proof of authentication; later successful source-case `su` is separate evidence. No hashes or logged credentials were used here.

Pages 15â€“17 contain mail clues, local services, key creation and forwarding, then a Gitea 1.22.0 browser demonstration. The messages are task data, not permission to send mail or change accounts. The source overwrites authorized_keys with `cp` and later names a different local key file without showing its transfer; neither was copied into a setup recipe. Existing SSH guidance already gives explicit loopback binds and connection checks. Gitea's official 1.22.1 announcement identifies CVE-2024-6886 and its fix; the historical footer alone is not a current vulnerability verdict.

Pages 18â€“19 send a review link, fetch a private-repository file through a browser session, decode a not-found response, then fetch a different file and reuse a discovered value. The mail clue names `README.md`, while the failed request uses `readme.md`; case-sensitive repository paths are a plausible additional explanation, so the failure does not establish absence of the named README. The script does not preserve the original fetch status. A callback's 200 is the collector's response status, and successful base64 decoding can merely recover an error body. Existing curl/base64 guidance covers that evidence distinction. Browser-session actions, private-file exfiltration and root credential reuse were deliberately not turned into utility defaults or executed. Sendmail instructions support an independently authorized message and explicitly distinguish queueing from delivery/opening.

**Primary verification.** [Git-dumper documentation](https://github.com/arthaud/git-dumper) and [implementation](https://github.com/arthaud/git-dumper/blob/master/git_dumper.py) support URL normalization, denied-listing recovery, request options, TLS behavior, file skipping, config rewriting and automatic checkout/status handling. [Git fsck](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-fsck) defines object checks and missing/dangling diagnoses. [GNU timeout source/help](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/src/timeout.c) supports the outer deadline, interrupt/kill interval and exit statuses; the GNU manual page was unavailable. A sandboxed local timeout help invocation returned nonzero without usable help, so it was not counted as runtime validation.

The [Sendmail manual distributed in FreeBSD's source tree](https://github.com/freebsd/freebsd-src/blob/stable/13/contrib/sendmail/src/sendmail.8) supports `-i`, `--`, `-t`, envelope sender/recipient distinctions, queue listing versus processing, and exit interpretation. Attempts to retrieve the Postfix manual failed, so the package explicitly scopes its administrative guidance to Sendmail 8 rather than claiming universal compatibility.

README catalogue entries were updated. Both new packages contain only their own SKILL.md and have no shared runtime dependency. Existing SSH forwarding, John key-format handling and scan guidance already cover their corresponding tasks; no redundant examples or separate Web3 SDK package were added.

**Page coverage and source qualifications.** Pages 1â€“2 introduce the two Ethereum-backed applications, IPFS and filesystem slack. Page 3 shows an all-TCP scan followed by selected-port service/default-script probing. Anonymous FTP returns Solidity source, a JSON artifact and an address file; an unclassified port is not itself proof of Ethereum. The existing scan guidance already handles scope and uncertain service classification.

Pages 4â€“5 show a string getter and setter and their ABI descriptions. An ABI specifies encoding/decoding; a matching filename does not prove that it describes deployed bytecode at a particular address. Pages 6â€“7 construct a Web3.py client, select the first exposed account and read a getter. Client construction does not load or verify every storage value, and an account in an RPC list is not proof of an unlocked signer. The old camelCase API is generation-specific; it was not copied into a new Python skill. The Cast adaptation checks the chosen chain/address/block and separates decode or missing-state errors from valid values.

Page 8 submits a transaction, reads the updated string and shows two ICMP request/reply pairs in tcpdump. The changed value and observed traffic are separate evidence stages; a submitted transaction hash is not by itself a mined successful receipt, and a getter does not prove an operating-system consumer executed the returned text. The historical local chain may mine immediately; portable guidance must not assume that timing. Page 9 shows a reverse-shell identity and a passwd excerpt. Contrary to the prose claiming only bobby has a Bash shell, the screenshot also assigns `/bin/bash` to administrator. Account shell metadata is separate from current SSH access policy. No payload or network probe was executed.

Page 10 enumerates the local IPFS store, loops over CIDs with `ipfs ls` and suppresses errors. IPFS does not require a blockchain, contrary to the source's description. The historical `Qm...` inventory representation differs from current Kubo's raw-codec CIDv1 inventory; not every stored block is a complete named file or UnixFS directory. The new guidance retains errors and obtains correctly typed root CIDs from known references/pins/MFS rather than blindly replaying the loop. A missing HTTP gateway does not by itself establish that all CLI operations stay offline.

Page 11 shows a multipart email's header excerpt, followed by a claimed extracted attachment decode and SSH-key recovery. The displayed header excerpt is insufficient to reproduce the exact attachment extraction: the part body and relevant part headers are omitted. `X-Attached` and `.enc` do not establish Content-Transfer-Encoding or encryption. Base64 decoding is separate from parsing/decrypting the resulting key; MIME tools may already have decoded it. The John output warns of possible candidate false positives. Page 12 then shows a distinct successful SSH identity observation; no recovered secret or authentication was reused here.

Page 13 shows a root-owned SUID executable and contract source containing application state. A failed password search does not establish that a hash cannot be cracked. Pages 14â€“15 show an application credential rejection, a generated address file, a loopback listener, SSH local forwarding and SCP. The unprivileged netstat output explicitly lacks some process attribution. A listening socket and a functioning forward do not independently establish the application protocol; the existing SSH package already explains both ends and destination failures.

Page 16 hardcodes a different contract address from the address displayed on page 14, despite prose saying it came from that file. Portable instructions use the actual deployment evidence. Pages 16â€“17 change application credentials and then receive an approval failure. Page 18 changes approval and receives an insufficient-funds message; these responses describe different application checks, not a universal login model. Pages 18â€“19 show a transfer predicate requiring a positive amount no greater than the remaining totalSupply. The page 19 explanation reverses the comparison in prose. Its contract balance is application state, not automatically the account's native-currency balance, and rerunning the same transfer after supply changes can behave differently. The later root `id` is an independent observed outcome of the source's SUID program. No contract transaction, financial transfer or SUID execution was performed.

Pages 19â€“20 compare a logical file read with `bmap --mode slack`. The shown file size is 52 bytes, filesystem block size 4096 and trailing slack 4044. This concerns bytes after EOF in an allocated filesystem block, not slack in RAM. Copying the logical file normally does not retain that original allocation/tail. The skill's arithmetic example is labelled illustrative and does not claim a recovered artifact. The source's final fragment is a finding within that lab, not a generally valid interpretation of any readable slack bytes.

**Primary verification, reviewed 2026-10-10.** The [Kubo CLI reference](https://docs.ipfs.tech/reference/kubo/cli/) verifies offline mode, timeouts, local inventory, recursive-pin listing, MFS listing/stat, UnixFS ls and cat byte limits. The [refs source](https://github.com/ipfs/kubo/blob/master/core/commands/refs.go) and CLI notes qualify raw block inventory and possible online retrieval. [Basic CLI operations](https://docs.ipfs.tech/how-to/kubo-basic-cli/) distinguishes directories and files; [IPFS concepts](https://docs.ipfs.tech/concepts/what-is-ipfs/) supplies the content-addressed model. No repository was initialized, migrated, locked, pinned, fetched or garbage-collected during review.

Daniel Ridge's [bmap source copy](https://github.com/CameronLonsdale/bmap) records its legacy provenance and a 2017 architecture/alignment patch. Its [bmap.c](https://github.com/CameronLonsdale/bmap/blob/master/bmap.c) verifies the read-only raw-device open for slack mode, regular-file check, terminal-block calculation, source-mutating alternate modes, append behavior of `--outfile` and unchecked raw I/O/exit-status limitations. That content password is not proof of account login or administrator access. Case credentials were not reused or copied into runtime instructions.

Page 7's command says port 995, whereas page 3 classifies 995 as POP3 and 993 as IMAP; the following screenshot is clearly an IMAP conversation. This internal inconsistency cannot establish a special port mapping. The new reference requires the actual endpoint/greeting and distinguishes 993 implicit TLS from IMAP STARTTLS. The source's shell-style trailing comments are annotations, not valid generic protocol input. An empty INBOX does not cover the Drafts folder. Page 8 shows MIME part headers, but not the complete two encoded attachment bodies; exact source-file recovery cannot be reproduced from that excerpt.

Pages 8â€“10 describe a 16-character zero-filled decimal byte count followed by a 16-byte IV and CBC ciphertext. The code uses a 65,536-byte read buffer, despite page 9 incorrectly describing 64*1024 bits as 16 bytes. Padding applies when the chunk length is not a multiple of 16, not merely when a chunk is shorter than 16. The source's SHA-256 digest is a 32-byte AES key. The original length is significant for removing space padding; calling it insignificant on page 10 loses that information. The decryption listing's text-mode open is not suitable for Python 3 binary ciphertext. A missing IV does not universally prevent recovery of every CBC block: later blocks depend on the preceding ciphertext. The added interpretation reflects that limit without treating unauthenticated output as trustworthy.

Page 11 prints readable inner base64 output followed by invalid input. Space padding plausibly explains the source symptom, but the supplied encrypted attachment is absent and was not reconstructed. The accepted workflow validates the established envelope, retains exactly the recorded original bytes, then checks the inner decoder's status. A visible plaintext prefix is not complete success. The local synthetic tests below independently verified the partial-output behavior; they do not reproduce the source artifact.

Pages 12â€“14 show a PDF web form, JavaScript/Ajax request, pdfTeX log, blacklist rejection, a different execution primitive and a shell. The log explicitly shows write18 enabled. The page 10 screenshots explicitly contrast recursive copying with `--remove-destination -p` against `--remove-destination --no-preserve=mode,ownership`. The latter deliberately resets mode/ownership behavior; it is not equivalent to plain cp -r. Existing versus newly recreated destinations, umask, ACLs and parent-directory access matter. The new guidance uses a fresh private outer directory and archive preservation, then checks selected file metadata separately from bytes. Archive mode is not a consistent live-application snapshot and can suppress some extended-attribute/context preservation failures. Copying source/. can replace destination-directory metadata, so the private outer layer is retained when containment matters.

Pages 10â€“11 show a Base32 seed followed by a TOTP_AUTH configuration line, and then oathtool output with a leading zero. Only the seed is key input; the complete configuration file is not a Base32 key. Page 10's prose misspells the utility name, while page 11 shows oathtool. Code generation and the later successful SSH identity are separate evidence. The accepted skill requires known provisioning parameters and avoids secrets in arguments or verbose logs.

Page 11's sudo rule and Bash wrapper lead into page 12's checker outcomes. Sourcing .env executes shell code; a C getenv call additionally requires the relevant variables to be exported. The wrapper's filtered username does not establish trust in later data. A match against a particular leaked-hash list does not establish comprehensive password safety when no match is found. The HTTP server exposes its served directory, including configuration and hash files in the listing. No transfer-integrity hash is shown. These conditions are recorded without reproducing the service or transferring files.

Page 13's decompiled main obtains environment variables and enforces a maximum strlen of 0x14 bytes, not a universal twenty-character Unicode rule. Its database lookup fetches a password-hash field; a null result's meaning depends on omitted error handling. Page 14's main writes the shared-memory value, flushes output, sleeps, then calls notification and cleanup. This contradicts page 16's prose placing the write after the sleep. The source's 0x400 request is 1,024 bytes. The first shmget argument is a key; its return is the segment ID. Linux flag value 0x3b6 separates into IPC_CREAT and permissions 0666, not a sticky-bit file mode. IPC_EXCL is absent, so source alone does not prove that a fresh segment was created. ipcs provides a bounded way to inspect actual metadata; it was not run here.

Page 15 writes a timestamp/hash string, then reads and searches delimiters. The `+1` after the delimiter pointer already skips that delimiter before the trim helper; attributing the entire operation to trimming is inaccurate. Pages 16â€“17 contain an attack helper that changes shared memory and appends unchecked data. Its shmget flags do not reassign an existing segment's ownership or permissions. The helper was not compiled or executed. The subsequently constructed mysql invocation crosses OS-shell, client-command and SQL parsing layers; the system command runs under the client process on the client host, independently of server FILE privilege. Filtering the wrapper's username cannot sanitize the later shared-memory input.

Page 18 redirects output to a path called pipe, but does not demonstrate that the path is a FIFO. Buffering and scheduling prevent treating the displayed sequence as a reliable universal race recipe. The displayed SUID file mode and a later process's effective UID are separate observations. The May 31 file timestamp differs from the May 24 shared-memory display and May 28 cover date; the screenshots should not be treated as one verified timeline. No race, shell payload, permission change or privileged execution was performed.

**Primary verification, reviewed 2026-10-10.** The [OATH Toolkit manual](https://oath-toolkit.codeberg.page/oathtool.1.html) verifies stdin/file key input, Base32 versus hexadecimal, HOTP/TOTP modes, algorithms, time parameters and verbose-secret exposure. [RFC 6238 Appendix B](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6238.html#appendix-B) supplies the public SHA1 test vector (59 seconds, eight digits, expected 94287082); its clock/step requirements support the mismatch decision. This is a published reference value, not a locally captured result.

The upstream-authored [ipcs manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man1/ipcs.1.html) verifies resource/ID selection, mutually exclusive display formats and procfs fallback visibility. The [shmget manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/shmget.2.html), [Linux IPC flag header](https://github.com/torvalds/linux/blob/master/include/uapi/linux/ipc.h), [shmat/shmdt manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/shmat.2.html) and [IPC namespace manual](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man7/ipc_namespaces.7.html) establish key/ID separation, creation versus permission bits, existing-segment behavior, attach/detach PID semantics and namespace scope. Metadata is not segment-content or last-writer evidence.

GNU's web manual could not be fetched directly. The [upstream coreutils manual source](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/doc/coreutils.texi), saved under ignored work, and the upstream [cp option parser](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/src/cp.c) / [copy implementation](https://github.com/coreutils/coreutils/blob/master/src/copy.c) verify preservation limits, destination removal and explicit non-preservation. The copy implementation applies default regular-file read/write permissions filtered by umask for newly created destinations under explicit no-preserve-mode. The manual distinguishes this from ordinary source-mode creation and existing destination behavior. No downloaded source was built or executed.

The [MySQL client-command manual](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-commands.html) and [client options](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/mysql-command-options.html) verify the local system command, formatting flags, noninteractive binary-mode exceptions and the 8.4.3/8.4.6 control additions. These version-specific controls are not assumed for MariaDB or historical clients; disabling client commands does not make arbitrary SQL harmless.

**Page coverage and source qualifications.** Page 1 introduces two historical library vulnerabilities and a two-stage Nmap command. Its first scan does not request every TCP port; two displayed open services therefore do not establish complete TCP/UDP coverage. Page 2 identifies observed SSH/Werkzeug banners and shows registration/login followed by the CIF upload dashboard. Registration and upload mutate the application; a web-server banner does not identify the exact installed pymatgen dependency. Page 3's vulnerability screenshot and adapted CIF place an expression in a crystallographic transformation field. The root cause is unsafe evaluation inside a parser, not a rule that all text-based CIF files or all deserializers execute code. The accepted Python addition traces the actual library call and deployed version without parsing the suspect file.

Page 3's shell payload uses callback port 9000, while page 4's listener is on 9090. No intervening port mapping or correction is shown, so the transcript is not directly reproducible as printed. The page 4 uploaded-file screenshot shows a View action and the narrative associates that with parsing; merely accepting an upload does not independently establish execution.

Page 4 prints `script -c /dev/null bash`, reversing the intended roles for util-linux script: /dev/null becomes command text and bash becomes the transcript filename. The displayed prompt alone does not validate that invocation or complete terminal behavior. The existing skill already has the correct command and now makes argument roles explicit. The source's SQLite query requests every column from a user table and its continuation on page 5 contains fourteen records. The database file itself is not supplied. Existing sqlite3 guidance prefers read-only working copies, schema inspection and bounded structured output; splitting default output on a delimiter can corrupt fields or lose account association.

Page 5 shows four recovered candidates with Hashcat mode 0, an account-file grep and an SSH invocation followed by a rosa prompt for socket inspection. The hash display's length alone does not prove raw MD5, and matching a database hash is separate from current SSH acceptance. Filtering passwd for /bin/bash excludes other valid shell configurations. The ss display's Local Address column establishes a 127.0.0.1:8080 listener; the peer wildcard does not make it externally bound. Missing process details do not identify the owner. The forwarding command's destination loopback is resolved on the SSH server; current ssh/ss skills already cover binding, forwarding policy and application checks.

Page 6 claims authentication to the forwarded monitoring application and shows its dashboard, followed by an aiohttp 3.9.1 banner. The later Feroxbuster/curl commands do not show session credentials, so one cannot infer that each reused the browser's authenticated session or that all routes require authentication. The maintainer advisory requires a particular static-route configuration for CVE-2024-23334; a banner alone is insufficient. The scan reports automatic 404-like filtering and individual CSS resources, while /assets returns 403. Page 7 continues with accessible JavaScript children and denied parent paths. These results are compatible with disabled directory indexes; they do not establish the filesystem root or a vulnerability by themselves. Recheck a known child and a control under the same request context before changing filters or expanding discovery.

Page 7's displayed Bash conditional contains a Markdown-link-style suffix after the closing bracket. The defect is visible in the rendered PDF, not solely text extraction. It is not a directly executable Bash example as printed. Its loop discards one response body while reading status, then makes a second request for content. That pairs evidence from different transactions. The added curl guidance captures all response evidence in one fetch and explains the outgoing path change caused by --path-as-is. The source's three-ancestor success is case-specific and does not reveal a universal static-directory depth.

Pages 7â€“8 show a flag-like body and a truncated private-key block from paths outside the web root. Those displays support the source's claimed read primitive but do not independently identify the serving process as root or demonstrate shell execution. Page 8 ends with key permissions and an SSH command; it provides no resulting authenticated identity output. The incomplete key cannot be validated or used as a complete artifact, and no credential acquisition or login was attempted during ingestion.

Those are not harmless fuzz cases. The strings output contains fragmented path/command text interleaved with extra characters; it guides disassembly but does not alone establish a complete executable command or code path.

Page 11 traces action 4, which the preceding README says deletes users. The observed setreuid call fails with EPERM, then access(path, R_OK) fails with EACCES; the program prints a combined unreadable/not-found message and exits zero. The trace proves an attempted permission check in that context, not a successful read or absence of the file. Ptrace can suppress set-ID transitions, and access normally checks real rather than effective IDs. A working privileged run cannot be inferred from this failed traced run. Retrying the same action without tracing could have destructive effects. The later path-traversal command shows a snipped private-key block, not a complete local key artifact. Page 13 prose names uppercase HTTP_PROXY while page 14's actual sudo invocation sets lowercase http_proxy. curl accepts the HTTP proxy environment variable only in lowercase on Linux; Windows environment-name behavior is different. Page 14 shows curl/7.81.0 through a Burp listener, a modified XML response with an external-entity declaration and a later root SSH id transcript. The proxy's displayed destination address differs from the earlier scan address, so those observations must keep their individual session context. Page 9 shows copying/editing that configuration and invoking npbackup 3.0.1 as root with backup/force flags. The output warns that filesystem snapshot mode is Windows-only. On Linux this warning does not establish application-consistent source acquisition. It reports processed source bytes separately from added/stored bytes; those are different quantities. **Page coverage and qualifications.** Pages 1â€“3 introduce the Windows scenario, selected service results and named Guest SMB access. The scan includes snipped results and a roughly six-hour TLS-derived offset, not proof of current SNTP reachability or a universal Kerberos tolerance. The named Guest attempt is not automatically a null session. Pages 3â€“4 show share browsing and recursive downloads; an empty mask, recursive state and remote directory selection are client-specific behavior, already addressed by smbclient guidance.

Pages 4â€“5 decompile a managed executable. Its entrypoint takes a basename, changes the extension and seeds System.Random from Unix seconds. It fills the IV before the key on one generator. Pages 6â€“7 read the remote output's last-write time through an SMB mount and use it as the candidate seed. That value is not creation time or a guaranteed exact encryption-start time. The source's serverino explanation is imprecise: it selects server identifiers, not freshly generated unique IDs. Its ntlmsspi description omits forced signing; vers=3.0 pins an SMB dialect. The source's writable generic /mnt mount was not copied into the skill; the existing dedicated read-only workflow remains.

Pages 8â€“9 show a edited decryptor with a hardcoded seed and FileMode.Create. Its loop uses actual bytes read; no stream-overread bug was inferred here. Output overwrite, partial decryption and .NET PRNG compatibility remain meaningful risks for any reconstruction. The supplied executable and encrypted source file were not available as separate artifacts and were not reproduced or executed. Page 10 identifies a 7-Zip header and shows successful extraction of two entries. Header recognition is narrower than full archive integrity, and the KDBX extension is not unique to KeePassXC. The screenshot's 7z e flattens paths; existing archive guidance already covers extraction selection.

Pages 11â€“12 show a key-file dialog, stored database entries, a TeamCity hostname and subsequent two-factor screen. The CLI adaptation is conditional on known key-only protection; a nearby key file does not prove that no password component is required. Stored credentials and URLs are evidence of configuration, not current identity or resolution. No database export or authentication was performed.

Pages 13â€“16 show an encrypted Authenticator export, TypeScript/CryptoJS call paths, a Node guessing script and an import sequence. The outer encrypted key is decrypted to a WordArray and converted with default toString(), yielding hex text. That text is supplied as the inner AES passphrase; hex-decoding it into raw key material changes the operation. The inner secret is later decoded as UTF-8. The nearby Argon2 verifier does not prove the AES KDF uses Argon2. The example's alphanumeric/length heuristic is not strict Base32 validation or proof of successful remote login. No wordlist, source ciphertext, secret or guessing script was run; the accepted OpenSSL workflow requires an already-known exact password and established format.

Pages 17â€“18 show successful import, rejected TOTP and subsequent reported success after rdate changes the clock. Import success alone is not a matching server enrollment, and a rejected code alone does not diagnose skew. The new skill measures first, preserves -p, distinguishes UDP/123 from RFC 868 and leaves clock changes outside the diagnostic. Existing oathtool guidance already covers enrollment parameters and a public RFC reference vector.

Pages 19â€“21 identify the project's local VCS path, its developer-role permissions and a custom personal-build patch. The displayed patch changes one tracked PowerShell file. An ordinary git diff omits staged-only and untracked material, and a build submission is an execution step separate from making a patch. Page 22's callback supports that observed request, not every claim about unrestricted execution or antivirus behavior. Pages 22â€“23 describe an insecure ReverseSSH broker and show a later service-account shell identity; the connection ID belongs to that broker rather than being an ordinary OpenSSH host/account. Evasion, disabled handshake validation, payload transfer and remote execution were not adapted into reusable instructions or tested.

Pages 23â€“25 locate TeamCity change files and show an encrypted PowerShell value together with a decimal-byte key. The displayed diff is snipped, so removing plus signs from the screenshot cannot recover omitted bytes. A generic patch is not a complete file and headers/hunks must be kept distinct. The explicit -Key path is separate from default Windows DPAPI protection; no source credential recovery was performed. Page 26 shows a separate authenticated user identity and group token, while page 27's group description alone does not prove all effective template rights.

Pages 27â€“29 describe obfuscation and state that the .NET build failed despite leaving an executable. Artifact presence does not settle freshness or which target failed; no obfuscation or build was reproduced. The later collector transcript shows the source case ran an executable and generated output; it does not retroactively prove the earlier build was successful. Pages 30â€“31 show graph containment, group membership and two object-specific ACL entries. Containment is not itself authorization, and the trustee filter is not a complete effective-rights calculation.

Pages 32â€“33 combine template manipulation, computer-object creation and certificate enrollment. The text equates decimal 524288 with 0x8000; the correct flag is **0x80000**, while 0x8000 denotes another setting. Assigning the whole enrollment-flags attribute also differs from preserving other bits. No-output from an ACL command alone is not read-back verification. The certificate transcript reports a DNS name and no object SID. Page 34 shows subsequent TGT/hash recovery and a RemoteOperations denial followed by DRSUAPI output; an error in one phase does not establish failure of every later phase. Its proposed cleanup-script explanation for arbitrary errors is a hypothesis, not a universal retry instruction. Page 35 separately shows an Administrator session identity. These historical CA-issued-certificate steps are distinct from the synopsis's shadow-credentials/key-trust label; existing certipy guidance already makes that distinction. Current mapping conditions cannot be inferred from this 2023 transcript.

## Coverage repair after the CrossFit review â€” 2026-10-10

**Implemented under schema v0.8: 32 new independent tool packages and two existing packages enriched.** This corrects the policy that rejected useful tools for overlapping another tool, having a short invocation, or lacking a Linux fixture on the authoring host. It also restores supported operational actions that had been narrowed to inspection-only guidance. The user selects which packages to install; one package cannot be treated as a substitute for another package's independent discovery.

This was a repair of recorded coverage decisions using the already read writeups, retained extracts/page records and current primary documentation. It was not a fresh claim to have re-read every PDF, and it did not advance the fixed ingestion queue. The original reading/visual coverage is recorded in the first/batch reports and individual entries above. Restored originals for 21 relevant sources were fingerprinted without extraction: 17 matched recorded hashes; Absolute, Academy, Active and Acute have newly recorded hashes but no prior hash found by this comparison. Raw comparison details remain in ignored work storage. No original PDF was changed, moved or deleted during this repair.

Source observations, derived operational advice and verified interfaces remain distinct. In particular: a process can run even when WMI output retrieval fails; owner restoration can need more rights than taking ownership; membership changes do not refresh existing tokens; RBCD removal is not whole-attribute flushing; old generic script names do not establish current implementation identity; build/package operations can execute hooks; and logs may contain plaintext even if argv omits credentials.

### Verified semantics and corrections

The target is OpenBSD with custom services. The tools' Linux-client procedures are useful, but observed OpenBSD paths, login_yubikey, httpd/relayd and unveil behavior are not invented as Linux-image facts. The source's relay includes a WebSocket patch; it is not a stock proxy configuration recipe. Quiet statistics do not establish working TLS, and control TLS is distinct from upstream DNS TLS. stats and stats_noreset have different reset behavior; the exposed custom server omits normal inspection/removal commands, so a reversible forward test needs an independently established recovery route.

Application text ping/pong is distinct from WebSocket protocol control frames, and the next incoming frame is not automatically the selected request's result. GROUP_CONCAT can lose boundaries or truncate data; an abbreviated debug value or brittle comma/string split cannot certify a complete inventory. LOAD_FILE NULL is ambiguous across permissions, policy, path and server-side limits. Source cross-fit/crossfit hostname typos are not propagated. Browser/socket session writes and events require their actual token/subscription state.

The source calls a form POST with a custom CSRF header a simple request; that header requires a browser preflight. Origin-only OPTIONS is not the actual preflight when method/header fields matter. curl can model these HTTP messages but does not enforce or prove browser CORS behavior. A failed callback or login does not establish that an earlier API write never happened. Reflected unusual Origin output alone does not establish the allowlist implementation. Native WebSocket and Socket.IO/EIO framing are not interchangeable.

CommonJS lookup begins at the requiring file, not the terminal directory; ancestor node_modules precedes NODE_PATH. ESM ignores NODE_PATH. Log timestamps/owners are not execution-identity evidence. The canary uses effective UID where available; Windows test results do not prove a privileged Unix process was run. The source's JSON parse lies outside its displayed try block; error-handling claims were qualified.

The Yubisim parser loads a decimal insertion counter C, increments to C+1 on insertion and emits a button/session counter of 1. OpenBSD's backend persists the combined value `(usage << 8) | session`. An **illustrative** saved value 3841 means usage 15/session 1; loading insertion 15 generates combined 4097 for 16/1. Copying the backend's combined integer into the simulator insertion field makes an unnecessary jump and is not generalized advice. The simulator prints the OTP before saving updated state, so stdout can exist even when persistence fails. Public ID handling differs by backend; private-ID checks still matter. Old javax.xml.bind imports require a compatible existing build/runtime or dependencies because JAXB is absent from a bare modern JDK. No OTP was generated during authoring.

Important semantics were reviewed through primary documentation and upstream browser views, without saving further executable source downloads:

- [Unbound control manual](https://unbound.docs.nlnetlabs.nl/en/latest/manpages/unbound-control.html) and [configuration manual](https://unbound.docs.nlnetlabs.nl/en/latest/manpages/unbound.conf.html): TLS credentials, command behavior, forwarding/local-zone/cache and insecure-zone effects.
- [Node CommonJS](https://nodejs.org/api/modules.html), [createRequire](https://nodejs.org/api/module.html#modulecreaterequirefilename), [startup flags](https://nodejs.org/api/cli.html), [ESM](https://nodejs.org/api/esm.html#no-node_path) and [effective UID](https://nodejs.org/api/process.html#processgeteuid): resolution, startup and identity distinctions. [Socket.IO v2 client API](https://socket.io/docs/v2/client-api/), [client options](https://socket.io/docs/v4/client-options/) and [v2/v3 migration](https://socket.io/docs/v3/migrating-from-2-x-to-3-0/) ground the versioned conditional event driver.
- [FakeDNS](https://github.com/Crypt0s/FakeDns) and [its matcher/parser](https://github.com/Crypt0s/FakeDns/blob/master/fakedns.py): rule syntax, transitions and the unused parsed flag. [Yubisim](https://github.com/dorchain/yubisim) and [implementation](https://github.com/dorchain/yubisim/blob/master/yubi_simulator.java), [OpenBSD login_yubikey](https://man.openbsd.org/login_yubikey.8), [backend implementation](https://github.com/openbsd/src/blob/master/libexec/login_yubikey/login_yubikey.c) and [Yubico OTP fields](https://developers.yubico.com/OTP/OTPs_Explained.html): token state, encoded counter and validation constraints.
- [Java launcher](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/java.html), [javac](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/docs/specs/man/javac.html) and [removed components](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/21/migrate/removed-tools-and-components.html): classpath, compilation and removed-library behavior.
- [websocket-client core API](https://websocket-client.readthedocs.io/en/latest/core.html), [curl cookie handling](https://curl.se/docs/http-cookies.html), [CORS](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS), [MySQL LOAD_FILE](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/string-functions.html#function_load-file) and [GROUP_CONCAT](https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/aggregate-functions.html#function_group-concat): transport/session and result boundaries.
- [PHP local server](https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.commandline.webserver.php), [Ncat manual](https://nmap.org/book/ncat-man.html), [Git clone](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-clone), [objdump](https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/binutils/objdump.html), [OpenBSD sshd_config](https://man.openbsd.org/sshd_config) and [unveil](https://man.openbsd.org/unveil.2): execution/configuration/import constraints. ### Important evidence and semantic corrections

The source's response differential reaches distinct application branches; it does not itself authenticate a user. The displayed source code uses `Cannot login`; nearby prose contains a different marker. The original username loop has no no-match exit and accepts the first match. The authored routine instead checks exact completion and unique branches within a stated request/length budget, with controls in the transport callback. `pager` uses telephone-number syntax/matching, not a universal numeric secret type; uid can be case-insensitive. Presence, substring and equality ask different questions. A reported false result can reflect grammar, authorization or application behavior rather than absence from the directory schema.

Percent decoding is a transport/application layer; RFC 4515 filter escaping is a different operation. Requests must prepare through the actual Session to apply cookies/headers. The examples distinguish a prepared wire body from sending through an authenticated session; timeout values alone do not impose a whole-response wall-clock limit. Source rate-limit avoidance by a one-second delay is an observation, not a general policy.

The group-filter reconstruction and embedded-NUL behavior on pp. 12â€“13 are historical application/binding hypotheses without supplied enclosing filter code or matching library/version evidence. The observed harmless identity response supports that source's command result. It does not establish a general LDAP truncation rule or a transferable bypass. The reference retains these conditions and the controlled comparison needed to investigate them; it does not invent a universal filter recipe.

The source archive banner is **p7zip 16.02**. Its log demonstrates listfile text interpreted as missing paths after `--`; current 7-Zip stops @listfile parsing after that switch. The upstream parser and maintainer's version discussion ground the difference. `-snl` controls link storage and is not protection from opening a selected listfile. Missing-path log strings do not prove every source byte was copied into the archive; archive encryption does not hide diagnostics. The root-file extension is claimed in source prose without a separate root-read transcript. Current unprivileged Windows fixtures below establish the modern argument boundary, not the source's privileged Linux symlink behavior.

- [stoken usage](https://github.com/stoken-dev/stoken#usage), [manual](https://github.com/stoken-dev/stoken/blob/main/stoken.1) and [prompt/time source](https://github.com/stoken-dev/stoken/blob/main/src/cli.c): raw compressed token inputs, selected config, local state, prompt/batch and absolute/relative time rules. `--stdin` supplies one required input; it is not an automatic two-prompt stream. `--next` and `--use-time` are mutually exclusive.

An older numeric-output option description was not propagated into current syntax.

Installed 26.03 help/format output and inert operations provide the Windows execution evidence below.

### Verified semantics, corrections and evidence boundaries

The archive sequence in this particular source is normal xxd dump â†’ bzip2 â†’ gzip â†’ bzip2 â†’ tar â†’ one password-like member. The reusable guidance identifies/tests each actual layer and retains complete status instead of guessing the sequence. Both decompressors can pass noncompressed data through with force/stdout, and truncated input can emit bytes before failure. A successful xxd reverse exit or readable inner file does not certify full source coverage. The published source's passwords and callback addresses are omitted from runtime material.

curl config is CLI input, not a constrained URL list. Output options pair with URLs in order: in the owned current-version fixture, output from the config was selected and an appended -o report did not replace it. --get encodes data into the URL rather than ordinary POST form bytes; the server decides whether the decoded value executes. A -q first argument skips only default curlrc, leaving explicit -K active. FILE support and protocol policy are distinct from read/write permissions. The source shows group-writable config mode and a command that resets its content after a delay; these are consequential race/restoration conditions. Page 10 shows both the HTTP request and a callback id result with UID 0, but this is source evidence, not an authoring reproduction or an assumption from a root-owned filename.

The source's nc build is not supplied. Accepted OpenBSD-style guidance is explicitly conditional on installed help; no historical -lvp or shell-execution option is generalized across variants. rlwrap editing occurs locally. Python pty.spawn is Unix-only, returns wait-status bits and can continue after input EOF while its child waits. The selected Python server follows symlinks, so document-root selection alone is not confinement; directory indexes and no authentication matter when serving a transfer artifact.

Applicable prior primary verification for xxd/file/tar/pspy/SSH/Nmap/Base64/Wget was retained. GNU gzip online manual/source refreshes failed; installed GNU gzip help and owned integrity/concatenation/force cases establish the options/results actually used. Failed refreshes and a non-source GitLab response are not claimed source reviews. No executable source downloads were saved.

**Source observations versus corrections:** pp4/7 show response-size outliers and later protected pages; error outliers are not all accepted credentials. P8 attributes the broader symbol-filter claim to an IppSec video; the shown finite character list alone is not universal coverage. P9's filtered table includes a 500 anomaly, so HTTP success/failure must not be treated as raw TCP state. Its 11211 lead is followed by actual ASCII-protocol responses; a TCP bridge does not become UDP because a port-search screenshot mentions UDP.

P11's slab classes 16/26 and stock/users keys are this instance's allocation, not stable schema. Key enumeration can omit live items, and get can miss after expiry. The current protocol's older metadata-dump size description and current cachedump code differ; no fixed complete-dump guarantee is adopted. P12's replacement decodes only one entity; HTML length is not Memcached payload length, and quote-splitting pretty JSON is not a lossless account parser. P13 incorrectly calls CVE-2018-15473 a timing attack. Banner-only exposure and upstream's old affected-version header are not authoritative patch detection. P14 HashID prints several algorithms fitting the value, rather than uniquely identifying MD5. P15's `ldconfig -v` can mutate cache/links even when its output is piped into a directory-list filter; the nonmutating scan requires both `-N -X`. P16/19's directory-order explanation is conditional on the actual dependency/search/cache rules, not a universal `/tmp` precedence rule. P17's function-name explanation does not establish when the library is loaded: direct ELF dependencies can load before main. The command shown retrieves the executable; acquisition of the associated library is stated in prose, without a shown matching-library transfer command. P18's stack string must be connected to comparison operands and the branch, not accepted solely because the debugger displays it. Debugger/ldd evidence is not the actual setuid launch.

P19's C snippet omits proper declarations, error checks and valid portable argument vectors; `execve(..., NULL, NULL)` is a Linux allowance, not portable process guidance.
